{{Short description|Concept in Peirce's philosophy}}
'''''Universal rhetoric''''' is a central concept in [[Charles Sanders Peirce]]'s philosophy. According to Peirce, the main purpose of universal rhetoric is to consider questions of [[inquiry]] in the context of [[community]],<ref name="Liszka96p99">Liszka (1996) [https://books.google.com/books?id=7QwrDAvL8TcC&pg=PT99 p.99]</ref> and "the very origin of the conception of reality shows that this conception ultimately involves a COMMUNITY, without definite limits, and capable of a definite increase of knowledge."<ref>Lang, P. (2002) [https://books.google.com/books?id=g8xhAAAAMAAJ ''The semiotics of fate, death, and the soul in Germanic culture''] p.11, quoting from ''Collected Papers of Charles Sanders Peirce'', ''Volume 5, Pragmatism and Pragmaticism'' p.311</ref>

Peirce alternatively called it '''speculative rhetoric''',<ref name="Houser2002">Houser, Nathan (2002) [https://minerva.usc.es/xmlui/bitstream/handle/10347/1206/pg_013-034_agora21-2.pdf?sequence=1''PEIRCE’S PRAGMATISM AND ANALYTIC PHILOSOPHY: SOME CONTINUITIES''], 27 AGORA (2002), Vol. 21, n° 2; 11-32</ref> '''general rhetoric''', '''formal rhetoric''', '''objective logic''', or '''methodeutic'''.<ref name="Liszka96p80">Liszka (1996) [https://books.google.com/books?id=7QwrDAvL8TcC&pg=PT80 p.80]</ref> It constitutes the third and last branch of his general [[Semiotics|theory of signs]].<ref name="Houser2002"/><ref name="Liszka96p80"/>
